strengths: The paper introduces a novel and timely problem formulation -- 'token sample complexity' -- which cleanly separates the effect of increasing context length at inference time (with fixed trained weights) from classical sample complexity in training. This is a useful conceptual contribution given the rapid growth of context windows in LLMs.

The technical core is substantial and rigorous: the authors adapt empirical process theory (symmetrization, Dudley's entropy integral, chaining for vector-valued sub-Gaussian processes) to handle the key difficulty that queries, keys, and values are drawn from the same finite token set, inducing nontrivial autocorrelation between the attention operator and the aggregated statistic. This is explicitly and convincingly contrasted with the concurrent work of Boursier & Boyer (2025), which does not face this coupling.

The progression from a naive compact-support bound (exponential in R, Theorem 4.2/naive moment bound) to the refined sub-Gaussian analysis (Theorem 5.3, polynomial dependence on scale, rate n^{-β}) is a genuine and non-trivial technical achievement, with a clear proof strategy (radius truncation and balancing of approximation vs. tail error).

The hardmax/infinite-horizon regime (Proposition 5.5) gives an elegant, exact asymptotic result (rate 1/√ln n) via extreme value theory, including a clean explanation of the cancellation phenomenon for symmetric Gaussian inputs, which sharpens intuition about worst-case slow convergence.

Empirical validation is reasonably thorough: synthetic Gaussian experiments closely match the predicted β = 1/(2(1+Ψ)) scaling across a range of horizons, and real-data experiments with BigBird across multiple languages/domains (English, German, Chinese Wikipedia, CC-News) and across 12 layers consistently show sub-parametric convergence rates that degrade with horizon and anisotropy, qualitatively matching the theory's predicted slowdown mechanism.

The appendix includes a careful sharpness analysis for a simple two-point (Dirac mass) example (Theorem B.11), showing the main bound is not tight in R and R0 in that special case, and providing a polynomial-rate alternative -- demonstrating honest engagement with bound quality rather than merely stating unverified claims.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.3 (the paper's main practical contribution) still yields a bound with substantial constants and a restrictive sample-size threshold (n ≥ 4(1/δ-1)n^{1/8}), and does not provide an explicit closed-form dependence of β on A and Σ for real (unknown) token distributions; the connection to the real-data BigBird experiments is therefore largely qualitative/post-hoc, relying on the general intuition of the sub-Gaussian mechanism rather than a directly verified fit of the theoretical formula.

Tightness of the general sub-Gaussian bound is explicitly left open (as stated in the conclusion); only very special cases (two Dirac masses, hardmax Gaussian limit) have matching lower bounds, so it remains unclear how close the established upper bounds are to the true rate in most realistic settings, including the Gaussian case used in Section 6.1 experiments.

The theoretical results assume i.i.d. token sampling, which is a strong idealization for real text (tokens in a sequence are highly dependent and structurally correlated); while the authors acknowledge this and note empirical agreement, no theoretical or empirical stress-test of this assumption's impact is provided beyond the observed power-law fits.

The analysis is restricted to a single self-attention layer; real transformers stack many layers with residual connections, layer normalization, and feedforward blocks, so it is unclear how the derived rates compound or interact across depth, limiting the direct applicability of the theory to end-to-end model behavior (though the paper is transparent about this scope).

The real-text experiments rely on position interpolation to extend BigBird's context to ~500K tokens to build the reference distribution ν, which introduces potential distributional shift/artifacts from extrapolating positional embeddings beyond their trained range; this is not discussed as a possible confound on the reported convergence rates.

The concurrent, independent work of Boursier & Boyer (2025) covers closely related territory (measure-based token sample complexity), which somewhat tempers the claim of novelty, even though the paper articulates real technical differences (dependent tokens, moment convergence vs. Jacobian concentration, smaller β, hardmax asymptotics).

The presentation is very dense with heavy notation and many interleaved definitions/propositions, which, combined with the large number of constants (C, C', q, P, etc.) in the main bounds, makes it hard for a reader to quickly extract the practically relevant takeaway messages without extensive cross-referencing to the appendix.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored question (finite-context approximation error of attention relative to its mean-field/infinite-token limit) and clearly differentiates it from classical PAC sample complexity.

The theoretical treatment is technically substantial: a genuine effort is made to handle the self-referential dependency structure of self-attention (queries, keys, and values all drawn from the same context), which requires a non-trivial chaining/Dudley-integral argument (Theorem 4.2) beyond what is needed in independent concurrent work.

The sub-Gaussian moment-convergence result (Theorem 5.3) meaningfully improves on the naive compact-support bound by replacing an exponential-in-radius constant with a polynomial one, via a sensible bias-variance/truncation argument balancing uniform convergence and tail concentration.

The exact asymptotic analysis of the hardmax limit (Proposition 5.5), showing a 1/√ln n rate driven by extreme-value cancellation, is a nice, self-contained analytical result with a clear intuitive explanation (cancellation between max/min selection).

Empirical validation spans both controlled synthetic Gaussian experiments (with reasonably good quantitative agreement to predicted exponents) and a real transformer (BigBird-RoBERTa) across multiple languages and corpora, lending some practical relevance to the theory.
The paper is largely honest about limitations (non-tightness of the general sub-Gaussian bound, i.i.d. token assumption, lack of explicit dependence of rate on A/Σ for unknown token distributions).
weaknesses: There is a substantial and unexplained gap between the general sub-Gaussian rate β = 1/(2(1+32Ψ)) (Theorem 5.3) and the exact Gaussian-case rate β = 1/(2(1+Ψ)) derived separately (Appendix C.3/C.6.5); the factor of 32 appears to be an artifact of the proof technique (threshold-splitting/balancing step) rather than a meaningful quantity, which undermines confidence that the general theorem captures the 'true' dependence on attention geometry and anisotropy that the paper advertises as its main contribution.

Tightness of the central bound (Theorem 5.3) is not established theoretically; the paper only claims empirical consistency, and even this is checked on a narrow regime (Gaussian, low dimension for hardmax) with a fairly limited range of n in the real-data experiments (n ∈ [1000, 3000]), making the power-law exponent estimates from log-log linear fits potentially unreliable/noisy over such a short window.

The core i.i.d. token assumption is unrealistic for natural language, where tokens exhibit strong sequential dependence, non-stationarity, and semantic structure; the paper's claim that empirical trends 'suggest' robustness to this assumption is not substantiated by any theoretical argument or ablation isolating this effect.

The real-data experimental protocol is somewhat artificial: BigBird is extended via position interpolation far beyond its trained context (4096 → 500k tokens) to construct the reference distribution ν, which may introduce its own distortions (out-of-distribution positional embeddings) that are not disentangled from the token-sampling convergence phenomenon being studied.

The practical takeaway/significance for practitioners or for understanding long-context LLM behavior is thin: the paper mostly confirms that convergence is slower than 1/√n and correlates with horizon/anisotropy, but does not translate this into actionable guidance (e.g., for context-window scaling, sparsification design, or error budgets) beyond a qualitative connection to sparse-attention methods that the authors explicitly say their theory does not cover.

The writing and notation are dense and appendix-heavy (40+ pages of proofs), with many constants and polynomial prefactors left unspecified (e.g., P(√ln n, L0) in Theorem 5.3), which limits the interpretability and usability of the stated rates even for readers willing to engage with the technical content.

The 'token sample complexity' terminology, while explicitly distinguished from classical sample complexity, may still be viewed as somewhat oversold, since the object of study is simply the finite-n approximation error of a fixed, already-defined operator (closer to a Monte-Carlo/empirical-process convergence question) rather than a new complexity notion with independent theoretical status.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually novel and timely notion -- 'token sample complexity' -- that is clearly distinguished from classical PAC sample complexity, addressing a practically relevant question as context windows scale to millions of tokens.

Technically substantial theoretical contribution: uniform convergence of the attention map over sub-Gaussian token distributions (Thm 4.2) is proved via a non-trivial application of Dudley's entropy integral and chaining, correctly handling the autocorrelation induced by self-attention's shared query/key/value tokens (a subtlety the paper explicitly contrasts with concurrent work by Boursier & Boyer).

Moves beyond a naive exponential-in-radius bound to a refined sub-Gaussian analysis (Thm 5.3) yielding polynomial-in-scale constants and an interpretable rate exponent β tied to an 'attention horizon' H and anisotropy Ψ, which is conceptually appealing and empirically validated.

The hardmax/infinite-horizon analysis (Prop 5.5) deriving an exact 1/√ln n asymptotic via Gaussian extreme value theory is an elegant and non-trivial limiting result, clearly explained via the 'cancellation phenomenon.'

Strong empirical validation on two complementary fronts: synthetic Gaussian data confirming the predicted β(H) curve, and real BigBird-RoBERTa experiments across multiple languages/datasets showing qualitatively consistent sub-parametric slowdowns, including covariance convergence in the appendix.

Extensive, careful appendix with detailed, mostly self-contained proofs (symmetrization, Rademacher complexity bounds, covering numbers, sub-Gaussian tail controls) and explicit sharpness discussion (e.g., the two-Dirac-mass example showing the general bound's suboptimality in R).
weaknesses: Tightness of the main sub-Gaussian rate (Theorem 5.3) is only empirically supported and explicitly left open theoretically (except in the trivial two-point example); the paper does not establish matching lower bounds for general sub-Gaussian/Gaussian distributions beyond the special hardmax case.

The link between theory and the real-data experiments is only qualitative: the exponent β's dependence on A and Σ is not explicitly computable for real (non-Gaussian, non-i.i.d.) token distributions, so the real-data results can only confirm directional trends (slower-than-1/√n, horizon/anisotropy correlation) rather than quantitatively validate the derived formulas.

All theory assumes i.i.d. token sampling, whereas real text tokens are highly dependent sequential data; this mismatch is acknowledged but not rigorously addressed, leaving open how much the reported real-data agreement is coincidental versus principled.

Experiments use BigBird, a sparse-attention model, as a stand-in for the dense self-attention theory; the random token subsampling protocol is only loosely connected to BigBird's actual structured sparsity pattern, and the authors themselves note the theory 'does not cover' such sparsification methods.

The hardmax asymptotic analysis is restricted to the 1-D Gaussian case, and the authors note that real embeddings do not exhibit the predicted cancellation/saturation, somewhat limiting the practical takeaway of this otherwise elegant result.

The paper is very dense, with most technical substance deferred to a long appendix; the main text sometimes reads as a high-level summary, which may limit accessibility and complicate independent verification without significant investment.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated theoretical framework ('token sample complexity') that quantifies how quickly finite-context attention approaches its infinite-token (mean-field) limit, addressing a timely question given the push toward very long context windows.

Rigorous mathematical development: uniform convergence of the attention map for sub-Gaussian tokens via a careful adaptation of Dudley's entropy integral/chaining to the vector-valued, ratio-of-empirical-averages structure of softmax attention (handling the non-uniform-Lipschitz kernel and near-zero denominator issues).

The 'attention horizon' H = ||Σ^{1/2}AΣ^{1/2}||_2 is an elegant, interpretable quantity that cleanly unifies the effects of token anisotropy and attention parameters on convergence speed, and is empirically validated as the key driver of the slowdown.

Sharpens the naive O(C(R)/√n) bound (exponential in R, hence practically useless) into a sub-parametric O(C'(R)/n^β) rate with polynomial dependence on scale, via a nontrivial bias-variance/truncation argument (Theorem 5.3), plus an exact asymptotic analysis of the hardmax limit (1/√ln n) with an interesting cancellation phenomenon.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: synthetic Gaussian/sub-Gaussian experiments confirming tightness of theoretical exponents, real-data experiments on BigBird and BERT across multiple languages/domains (7 datasets), and an end-to-end downstream classification task tying the theory to practical accuracy/agreement metrics — with quantitative insight (e.g., 25% of keys recovering most dense-model accuracy).

Thoughtful additional results: sharp two-Dirac-mass example showing where the general bound is loose, a heavy-tailed counterexample showing sub-Gaussianity is necessary, an explicit discussion/experiment on the i.i.d. assumption via windowed sampling, and an appendix (E) improving the exponential-in-R dependence to polynomial under additional regularity.
Clear positioning relative to concurrent work (Boursier & Boyer, 2025), with explicit technical differences (same-token queries/keys/values dependency requiring chaining) highlighted.
weaknesses: The core theoretical setup assumes i.i.d. resampling of tokens from a fixed empirical/population distribution to model 'increasing context length'; this is a stylized proxy that does not directly capture how a real token sequence grows (tokens are ordered, dependent, and often not exchangeable). The windowed-sampling experiment partially mitigates this concern but does not extend the theory itself.

The single-attention-layer, no-positional-encoding, non-causal model is a simplification relative to real Transformers (though multi-head is covered and empirical validation uses full models); the gap between the idealized theoretical object and the actual layer being measured in BigBird/BERT is not fully bridged theoretically.

Constants and rates in the main theorems (e.g., Theorem 4.2, 5.3) are complex and, outside special cases (Gaussian, two-Dirac-mass), their tightness is not established; the paper acknowledges tightness of the general upper bound 'remains widely open.'

The downstream sparsification experiment uses i.i.d. random key subsampling as a stand-in for sparse attention, which is a considerable simplification relative to practical structured sparse-attention mechanisms (Longformer, BigBird's actual pattern, Linformer), somewhat limiting the direct practical takeaway despite the added windowed-sampling check.

Empirical convergence rates are estimated via log–log linear fits over a finite n-range per configuration; robustness/sensitivity of the fitted β to the choice of n-range and to departures from sub-Gaussianity in real text embeddings is not deeply analyzed.

The practical inference-time insight (diminishing returns after ~25% of keys) is qualitatively consistent with existing folk knowledge in the sparse-attention literature, so the incremental practical novelty is moderate even though the theoretical explanation is new.
The dense mathematical presentation (many nested lemmas/propositions in main text and ~40 pages of appendix) may reduce accessibility for a broader ICML audience despite the topic's relevance.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clear and reasonably novel question: how fast does attention computed on a finite token sequence converge to its infinite-token (measure-theoretic) limit, distinguishing it cleanly from classical PAC sample complexity.

Substantial and careful theoretical machinery: uniform convergence via Dudley's entropy integral with a non-trivial multidimensional/duality adaptation to handle the unbounded-envelope, non-uniformly-Lipschitz softmax kernel; moment convergence via a truncation/tail trade-off argument; and an exact extreme-value-theory analysis of the hardmax limit.

The 'attention horizon' H = ||Σ^{1/2}AΣ^{1/2}||_2 is an elegant unifying quantity that connects the theoretical rate exponent β to an interpretable geometric notion (largest achievable query-key score in the covariance geometry), and this quantity is shown empirically to organize convergence behavior across synthetic Gaussian data, two real pretrained models (BigBird, BERT), multiple languages/domains, and a downstream classification task.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: synthetic Gaussian experiments closely match the theoretical β(H) curve; real-data experiments across 12 BigBird layers and 7 text corpora show the predicted layer/horizon-dependent slowdown; an end-to-end downstream classification experiment ties the attention-level slowdown to accuracy/agreement degradation, which is a nice attempt to connect abstract theory to practical consequences.

Honest acknowledgment of some limitations (e.g., heavy-tailed counterexample to show sub-Gaussianity is necessary; explicit statement that real BigBird embeddings do not exhibit the predicted Gaussian-hardmax cancellation).
weaknesses: The central modeling assumption -- that queries/keys/values are n i.i.d. draws from a fixed 'token distribution' ν, and that increasing context length corresponds to drawing more i.i.d. samples from this same ν -- is a weak proxy for how context actually grows in practice (a single, structured, highly dependent sequence of tokens, not fresh i.i.d. draws). The paper itself admits this gap (windowed-sampling experiments and the i.i.d. discussion in Appendix A) but the core theory and most experiments still rely on i.i.d. subsampling from an empirical 'reference' distribution built from hundreds of thousands of real tokens, which only loosely models realistic long-context inference.

The practical motivation (extending context windows to millions of tokens) is not directly addressed: the downstream experiment demonstrates a sparse-attention-via-random-key-subsampling scenario, which is an artificial construction rather than a natural description of how dense attention over genuinely longer contexts would behave; the leap from 'random key subsampling slows convergence' to 'this explains limits on benefits of longer context windows' is asserted rather than rigorously justified.

The hardmax/large-A regime result, while mathematically elegant, is explicitly stated to not match real data behavior ('real token embeddings... do not display the above saturation'), undermining its practical relevance and leaving the paper's two main theoretical regimes (sub-Gaussian moments and hardmax limit) only partially connected to the empirical findings.

Several bound statements appear awkwardly or confusingly formulated, e.g., Theorem 5.3's probabilistic guarantee is stated to hold 'for n ⩾ 4(1/δ − 1) n^{1/8}', which has n appearing on both sides of the inequality -- an apparent typo/unclear threshold definition that is not resolved in the main text and raises concerns about the care taken in finalizing the formal statements.

The empirical fits to the predicted power law are only loosely consistent in the real-data experiments (e.g., Figure 4's layer/horizon scatter has considerable spread around the linear fit, R≈-0.64), and the specific functional form of H (itself dependent on a single global Σ and A per layer) is a simplification of highly structured, non-Gaussian, non-stationary real token distributions, making the quantitative claims less convincing than the synthetic Gaussian validation.

The paper's technical contribution, despite its length and depth, is largely an application of standard empirical-process/concentration tools (Dudley entropy integral, sub-Gaussian concentration, extreme value theory) to a specific nonlinear estimator (softmax attention); while the application is non-trivial, the conceptual novelty beyond 'softmax amplifies tails, hence slower than parametric rates, with rate governed by an effective Lipschitz/exponential growth parameter' is somewhat incremental relative to the very large volume of derivations.

The downstream validation is based on a single dataset/task (arxiv-classification with BigBird-RoBERTa), limiting confidence that the connection between the theoretical horizon-dependent slowdown and downstream task quality generalizes across architectures and tasks.

The Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate non-statement, reflecting limited engagement with potential implications (e.g., for efficient inference/sparsification claims made in the introduction).

strengths: Novel, well-motivated framing of 'token sample complexity' distinct from classical PAC sample complexity, directly relevant to long-context LLM deployment.

Technically substantial uniform convergence result (Theorem 4.2) handling a genuinely hard setting: unbounded envelope, non-uniformly-Lipschitz softmax kernel, and self-referential queries/keys/values drawn from the same token set, via a careful vector-valued Dudley chaining argument.

Introduction of the 'attention horizon' H = ||Sigma^{1/2} A Sigma^{1/2}||_2 as an interpretable, empirically validated quantity linking token covariance geometry and attention parameters to convergence rate.

Exact (not just upper-bound) asymptotic result in the hardmax limit (Proposition 5.5), with an elegant cancellation argument from Gaussian extreme value theory, plus a heavy-tailed counterexample showing necessity of sub-Gaussianity.

Extensive and consistent empirical validation across synthetic Gaussian data, multiple real corpora/languages, two different pretrained models (BigBird, BERT), window-based (non-i.i.d.) sampling robustness checks, and an end-to-end downstream classification task linking theory to accuracy/logit-error/agreement curves.
Clear positioning relative to concurrent independent work (Boursier & Boyer), explaining the distinct technical contribution.
weaknesses: The flagship downstream classification experiment uses a full multi-layer trained model with LayerNorm, residuals, and structured (non-i.i.d.) key sampling, which is not directly covered by the single-layer i.i.d. theory; the link between theory and this experiment is empirical/suggestive rather than a proven corollary.

Tightness of the general sub-Gaussian upper bounds is not established (acknowledged by the authors); only a simple 1-D two-point example and the Gaussian-specific sharper rate are analyzed, leaving open how loose the bound (exponent depending on 32H^2 vs. H^2 in the Gaussian case) is in realistic high-dimensional settings.

The i.i.d. subsampling assumption, while a reasonable simplifying model, does not match realistic sparsification strategies (local windows, causal masking, learned routing); the windowed-sampling experiment is a useful but limited robustness check without accompanying theory.

Constants and polynomial prefactors in the main theorems (e.g., P(sqrt(ln n), L0) in Theorem 5.3) are not made fully explicit in the main text, making practical token-count implications hard to assess without consulting the appendix.

Extension to multi-head attention is asserted rather than demonstrated in detail in the main text, and explicit connection to practical sparse-attention architectures (Longformer, Linformer, BigBird's actual sparsity pattern) is explicitly left out of scope.
